Q: What are high and low water marks in bit streaming A:

The answer from @cello is comprehensive. Mine is a just from another angle.

Imagine a water tank (buffer) with capacity of 100 gallons with high mark at 90 gallons and low mark at 35 gallons with two pipes connected to it:

  • producer pipe (media server) is quickly filling the tank.
  • consumer pipe (media player) is slowly draining the tank.

The issue is obvious - without controlling the water flow the tank will be overfilled quickly. High / low water marks are used to control the flow.

  • When 90 gallons are filled -> instruct producer to stop filling.
  • When draining reached 35 gallons -> instruct product to start filling.

This model allow to keep flows (bytes, blocks, pages) and buffers under control.

Q: SQL Server 2016 - Temporal Table - how to identify the user A:

An important thing to understand is that the username cannot be in the same table as the information.

Consider the following record:

EmployeeID FirstName ModifiedBy ValidFrom ValidTo
1 John admin 2026-01-02 15:00:00 2026-08-10 08:09:35

It says that admin modified the record, but what kind of action was it? It surely can't be an insert, because ValidTo is not year 9999, but both updates and deletes result in the same historical record. How do we know which is it?

For example, for the given set of actions:

  1. INSERT (FirstName = 'John')
  2. UPDATE (FirstName = 'Johnny')
  3. UPDATE (FirstName = 'Jonathan')
  4. DELETE

We have the following set of historical records:

EmployeeID FirstName ValidFrom ValidTo
1 John 2026-08-10 10:00:00 2026-08-10 10:01:00
1 Johnny 2026-08-10 10:01:00 2026-08-10 10:02:00
1 Jonathan 2026-08-10 10:02:00 2026-08-10 10:03:00

We have 4 actions but only 3 records. Where do we place the info? We could add CreatedBy and DeletedBy columns, but these names seem confusing considering an update is not “created” or “deleted”.

All of this, on top of the fact that you can't touch historical tables at all, leads me to a solution where an extra table holding this information is needed. And to fill this table, we need to add triggers to the original table.

So, the scripts would look like this:

CREATE TABLE Employee
(
    EmployeeID INT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY CLUSTERED,
    FirstName VARCHAR(MAX) NOT NULL,
    Score INT NOT NULL,

    ValidFromUtc DATETIME2 GENERATED ALWAYS AS ROW START HIDDEN NOT NULL,
    ValidToUtc DATETIME2 GENERATED ALWAYS AS ROW END HIDDEN NOT NULL,
    PERIOD FOR SYSTEM_TIME (ValidFromUtc, ValidToUtc)
)
WITH (SYSTEM_VERSIONING = ON (HISTORY_TABLE = dbo.EmployeeHistory));

CREATE TABLE EmployeeHistoryInfo
(
    --https://dba.stackexchange.com/a/343938
    --This guarantees the same datetimes from the history tables
    --are generated for our helper table.
    TimeUtc DATETIME2 GENERATED ALWAYS AS ROW START NOT NULL,
    MaxDateTime2 DATETIME2 GENERATED ALWAYS AS ROW END HIDDEN NOT NULL,

    [User] VARCHAR(MAX) NOT NULL DEFAULT (SUSER_SNAME()),
    EmployeeID INT NOT NULL,
    Action CHAR(6) NOT NULL,
    PERIOD FOR SYSTEM_TIME (TimeUtc, MaxDateTime2)
)

CREATE TRIGGER Employee_instrg
ON Employee
FOR INSERT
AS
    INSERT INTO EmployeeHistoryInfo (EmployeeID, Action)
    SELECT inserted.EmployeeID, 'INSERT'
    FROM inserted

CREATE TRIGGER Employee_updtrg
ON Employee
FOR UPDATE
AS
    INSERT INTO EmployeeHistoryInfo (EmployeeID, Action)
    SELECT inserted.EmployeeID, 'UPDATE'
    FROM inserted

CREATE TRIGGER Employee_deltrg
ON Employee
FOR DELETE
AS
    INSERT INTO EmployeeHistoryInfo (EmployeeID, Action)
    SELECT deleted.EmployeeID, 'DELETE'
    FROM deleted

And then, whenever you need to get info about who modified a record, you join the table EmployeeHistoryInfo with Employee. An example would be:

SELECT *
FROM EmployeeHistoryInfo
LEFT JOIN Employee FOR SYSTEM_TIME ALL
    ON 1 = 1
    AND EmployeeHistoryInfo.EmployeeID = Employee.EmployeeID
    AND EmployeeHistoryInfo.TimeUtc = Employee.ValidFromUtc
WHERE EmployeeHistoryInfo.EmployeeID = 1
ORDER BY EmployeeHistoryInfo.TimeUtc DESC
TimeUtc User EmployeeID Action EmployeeID FirstName Score
2026-08-10 16:33:54.3243893 admin 1 DELETE NULL NULL NULL
2026-08-10 16:33:43.9635904 admin 1 UPDATE 1 Jonathan 100
2026-08-10 16:33:32.5560761 admin 1 UPDATE 1 Johnny 100
2026-08-10 16:33:13.6785816 admin 1 INSERT 1 John 100

Q: How to reliably restart Web Speech API SpeechRecognition after <audio> playback on iOS Safari? [confirmed WebKit bug, fixed upstream] A:

Here's the issue. Thanks in advance if you have a solution or suggestion. =)

Root cause, confirmed: this is WebKit bug 317741 — "Speech recognition microphone source should make sure to keep its audio session active while capturing." A WebKit engineer (youenn fablet) confirmed it on WICG/speech-api#96 and the fix (commits 315887@main / 316394@main) has already landed upstream.

Current shipping status (as of August 2026): the fix is in Safari Technology Preview 248, but has not shipped to any stable Safari/iOS release yet — Safari 26.6 doesn't have it. So on a real device today, you'll still see this bug. Worth checking the webkit.org blog periodically — once it appears in a stable "WebKit Features for Safari X.X" post, this should just go away.

Workarounds that help in the meantime (none are a full fix, but combined they get you a usably-reliable mic):

  1. Auto-retry with escalating delays. A single retry with a fixed delay isn't enough — what actually works reasonably reliably is retrying up to ~4 times with growing delays (e.g. 300ms, 1000ms, 2000ms, 3500ms) after a failed/silent attempt. This mirrors what other reporters on the GitHub thread found ("restart and hope"), just automated.

  2. Prime with getUserMedia before the first attempt, not on every retry: await navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({audio:true}) then immediately stop the tracks, right before calling SpeechRecognition.start(). Only do this once (on the first attempt) — doing it on every retry adds audible mic-permission churn without helping more.

  3. Give it a real settle window after voice playback, not just a short fixed delay — waiting up to ~10s after your last TTS audio finished, before the first mic attempt, measurably improves first-attempt success. Retries after that don't need to wait nearly as long.

  4. If you don't need live/interim transcription, sidestepping SpeechRecognition entirely with MediaRecorder + a server-side STT API (Whisper, ElevenLabs Scribe, etc.) avoids this bug completely, since it never negotiates a live recognition session with WebKit. Trade-off: no live "words appearing as you talk" feedback, just record → upload → get text back.

  5. If your case is audio-playback quality/volume rather than the mic breaking, switching TTS playback from HTMLAudioElement to the Web Audio API (AudioContext.decodeAudioData() + AudioBufferSourceNode) resolved a closely related symptom for at least one other developer on the GitHub thread — worth trying if you're fighting quiet/cut-off playback specifically.

Also filed bug 321436 with our specific repro (breaks on the next start() after playback ends, not concurrent capture) in case it's a distinct variant from 317741.

Q: Understanding a mingw32 "arrays of functions are not meaningful" error A:

On some further checking I believe the cause is this macro: https://github.com/Rhekar/CCCaster/blob/master/targets/DllAsmHacks.hpp#L86-L90

#define INLINE_DWORD(X)                                                         \
    static_cast<unsigned char> ( unsigned ( X ) & 0xFF ),                       \
    static_cast<unsigned char> ( ( unsigned ( X ) >> 8 ) & 0xFF ),              \
    static_cast<unsigned char> ( ( unsigned ( X ) >> 16 ) & 0xFF ),             \
    static_cast<unsigned char> ( ( unsigned ( X ) >> 24 ) & 0xFF )

Specific when it's invoked like this: https://github.com/Rhekar/CCCaster/blob/master/targets/DllAsmHacks.hpp#L587

0xE8, INLINE_DWORD ( ( ( char * ) &addExtraTexturesCb ) - 0x41BE38 - 5 ),       // call addExtraTexturesCb

I guess all the nested parens and casts is confusing mingw to think this is an array of functions somehow.

Edit: I ended up solving this by replacing the "char *" casts with casts to the "uintptr_t" type. Replacing some of the integers with names constants or definitions also seems to work.

Q: What is the utility of ARM 64KB Large Pages? A:

From the ARM720 TRM,

Large Pages consist of 64KB blocks of memory. Large Pages are supported to allow mapping of a large region of memory while using only a single entry in the TLB). Additional access control mechanisms are extended to 16KB Sub-Pages.

The main benefit is a 64k entry will only consume one TLB (MMU page entry cache). The TLB is 64 entries so 64*4k = 256kB versus 64*64k = 4MB; a significant increase in the amount of memory that doesn't require a page table lookup to address.

There are many down sides. For instance, a portable OS (and it's API) might require the smaller pages. If all entries are 64k fragmentation can result. The section entries are even better with each representing a 1MB chunk with 64MB fitting in the TLB. Generally the section will work better for a virtual==physical mapping.

If you know your system only has 4MB of usable memory then the 64k page entries can result in more reliable performance. Even with larger memory sizes the interrupt code and data can use 64k entries with TLB lock down note to avoid page table walks. This can result in better IRQ latency. The TLB is a limited resource so using 4k entries for the interrupt handler may result in wasting the TLB. Using section entries may waste memory as most interrupt code is <1MB.

Even without lock down, it is more likely that a 64k entry that is frequently used will remain in the TLB. An OS with per task/process memory may need to change the MMU tables which can result in TLB and cache flushing and invalidate. In order to simplify the context switch, everything maybe invalidated and flushed. So a table walk on an interrupt may be more common than you would suspect. This is a motivation to use the MMU 'PID' functionality and to only flush/invalidate smaller regions of memory and allow kernel code/data to remain in system caches. Additional code like the scheduler will also benefit from being mapped by a 64k entry.

Note: The ARM720T may/may not have lock down, but some ARM CPUs do and the MMU entry are fairly similar between CPU families. This answer applies to many different families of ARM CPUs.
